In presence of acidic medium, ionisation of H2S is supressed so less number of S2- ions are produced. So only those sulphides are precipitated which have low solubility product Ksp value.

The probability that he/she copies the answer is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac></math>. If the probability that the answer is correct, given that he/she copied it is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>8</mn></mfrac></math>, then the probability that he/she knows the answer to a question given that he/she correctly answered it, is
questions.solution:
Let A be the event that the examinee gives the correct answer.

Let G, C, K stand for guessing, copying and knowing. respectively.

Given, PC=16, PG=13

and PAC=18

⇒PC+PG+PK=1

⇒16+13+PK=1

∴ PK=12

Also, PAK=1, for if the examinee knows, he/she will correctly answer it and PAG=14,

 since there are four choices.

Now, total probability PA=PGPAG+PCPAC+PKPAK

=13·14+16·18+12·1

=112+148+12=4+1+2448=2948

Now, PKA=PKPAKPA

=12·12948=12·4829=2429

questions.q: At a certain temperature, the number density of charge carriers in a semiconductor is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi></math>. When an electric field is applied to it, the charge carriers drift with an average speed <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>v</mi></math>. If the temperature of the semiconductor is raised.
questions.solution: On raising the temperature of the semiconductor, covalent bonds start breaking up and thus more charge carriers release. This will increase the value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi></math> and as a result the rate of collision of charge carriers will increase. This will decrease the drift speed <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>v</mi></math>.

questions.q: Steam at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>100</mn><mo> </mo><mo>°</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></math> is passed into <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>1</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi></math> of water contained in a calorimoter of water equivalent to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>2</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi></math> at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>15</mn><mo> </mo><mo>°</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></math> till the temperature of the calorimeter and its contents rises to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>80</mn><mo> </mo><mo>°</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></math>. The mass of steam condensed (in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>kg</mi></math> ) is
questions.solution:
(a) According to principle of calorimetry,
heat gained = heat lost
Heat is lost by steam in two stages

(i) Change of state from steam at 100 °C to water at 100 °C is m×540.

(ii) To change water at 100 °C to water at 80 °C is m×1×100-80, where m is the mass of the steam condensed.

Total heat lost by steam is
m×540+m×20=m 540+20=560 m

Heat gained by calorimeter and its contents is
1.1+0.2×80-15=1.12×65 cal 

⇒  560 m=1.12×65

⇒  m=1.12×65560=0.130 kg
